blocks.text:
Design the core of an online shopping service that prevents overselling without permanently locking inventory the moment someone glances at a product. When a buyer begins checking out, the requested quantity is tentatively reserved, decremented from available stock immediately, but only for a limited window of time. If the buyer completes checkout within that window, the reservation becomes a real order. If they abandon their cart or simply take too long, the reservation automatically expires and the stock returns to the available pool, whether or not anyone ever notices.

  • Actors: Buyer (reserves items, checks out), ShoppingService (the core orchestrator).
  • Scope: stock-aware reservation with expiry, checkout confirming a set of reservations into an order, coupon-based discounting, and automatic release of abandoned holds.

The distinguishing mechanic is a temporary, time-bounded inventory hold, not a permanent lock. Every prior booking-style problem in this set (hotel rooms, movie seats, concert tickets) held a resource permanently once claimed; here a hold is provisional and silently releases itself if nobody follows through.
The system must support the following core capabilities:

items: Reserve an item: a buyer requests a quantity of a product; if enough stock is available, it is decremented and held under a time-bounded reservation.
Checkout: a buyer confirms a set of active, unexpired reservations into a finalized order, with an optional coupon applied.
Automatic expiry: a reservation not confirmed before its expiry time is released, returning its held quantity to available stock.
Reject on insufficient stock: a reservation attempt that exceeds available stock is rejected with a clear reason.
Reject on expired checkout: attempting to check out with an already-expired reservation is rejected, and that reservation's stock is released immediately as a side effect.

blocks.text: Beyond correctness, the design should hold up along five quality pillars:

metadata.alt: Five non-functional pillars: scalability, extensibility, maintainability, performance, thread safety

items: Scalability: supporting many products, reservations, and orders must not require touching existing reservation logic.
Extensibility: a new discounting scheme should plug in without rewriting the service.
Maintainability: discounting, notification, and id creation are isolated in their own classes.
Performance: reserving stock and creating a reservation is O(1) via a direct product lookup.
Thread safety: two buyers reserving the last unit of a product concurrently must not both succeed.

blocks.text: Questions worth asking the interviewer before designing:

items: How long should a reservation hold stock before expiring, and is that window configurable per product?
Should the background expiry sweep run on a fixed schedule, or should expiry only be checked lazily when a reservation is next touched?
Can a single checkout span reservations for multiple different products at once?
Should a coupon code be validated against usage limits or eligibility rules, or is it purely a flat discount lookup for this design?
What should happen to a reservation if the buyer explicitly cancels it before its natural expiry?

blocks.text: To keep the design focused, we make these explicit assumptions:

items: A reservation holds stock for a fixed window (10 time units in this design's demo scale) from the moment it is created.

Expiry is checked both lazily, whenever a reservation is next touched by a checkout attempt, and eagerly, via a periodic background sweep, so stock is never held indefinitely even if nobody ever tries to check out.
A single checkout call can confirm reservations spanning multiple different products into one order.
A coupon code maps to a flat discount percentage via a simple lookup; usage limits and eligibility rules are noted as a future extension.
Explicit buyer-initiated cancellation before natural expiry is out of scope for this design, noted as a follow-up.

blocks.text: The design centers on three core entities:

items: Product: a catalog item with a price and available stock count.
Reservation: a time-bounded hold against a product's stock for a specific quantity.
Order: the finalized result of confirming one or more reservations at checkout.

blocks.text: These entities connect through a small set of well-defined relationships:

metadata.alt: A product has many reservations over time; a reservation becomes at most one order line once confirmed; an order references many products through its confirmed reservations

items: Product to Reservation is one-to-many.
Reservation to Order is zero-or-one, since a reservation only becomes part of an order once confirmed at checkout.
Order to Product is many-to-many, through its set of confirmed reservations.

Why needed: how a coupon code translates into a discount is a business rule that changes independently of how reservations and checkout work.

blocks.text: Why it is the best fit: a new discounting scheme (tiered discounts, buy-one-get-one) is a new strategy implementation, with zero changes to ShoppingService. What it solves: it isolates a frequently-changed promotional rule from stable checkout logic.
Why needed: reservation creation, rejection, order confirmation, and expiry are all events a real storefront would want to react to (cart abandonment emails, inventory alerts).

metadata.alt: ShoppingObserver interface notified by ShoppingService on every lifecycle event

blocks.text: Why it is the best fit: ShoppingService does not need to know who is listening. What it solves: it decouples the core reservation workflow from side effects.
Why needed: reservation and order id generation should not be scattered across calling code.

metadata.alt: ShoppingIdFactory generating sequential R and O prefixed ids

blocks.text: Why it is the best fit: every reservation and order is created through one consistent path. What it solves: centralizes id-generation rules so they cannot drift or collide.
Each class has a single, clear responsibility:

items: Product: attributes productId, name, price, availableStock; responsibility: track a catalog item's current sellable quantity.
Reservation: attributes reservationId, productId, quantity, expiresAt, status; responsibility: represent one time-bounded hold.
Order: attributes orderId, userId, totalAmount, status; responsibility: represent one finalized purchase.
ShoppingIdFactory: methods nextReservationId, nextOrderId; responsibility: generate sequential, correctly-prefixed ids.
ShoppingService: the orchestrator; responsibility: validate and create reservations, confirm checkouts, release expired holds, and notify observers.

blocks.text: Two interfaces keep the design open for extension:

metadata.alt: DiscountStrategy and ShoppingObserver interfaces with their key methods

items: DiscountStrategy: discountPercent(couponCode): returns the discount fraction to apply for a given coupon.
ShoppingObserver: onReservationCreated / onReservationRejected / onOrderConfirmed / onReservationExpired: abstracts away who reacts to lifecycle events.

blocks.text: Three flows below cover a successful reservation and checkout with a discount, a rejection for insufficient stock, and a checkout attempt on an already-expired reservation.

metadata.alt: Alice reserves a unit of P1 and checks out before expiry with a 10 percent coupon applied
Carol tries to reserve P1 when available stock has already reached zero
Bob attempts to check out after his reservation's expiry has passed, triggering an immediate stock release and rejection

blocks.text: The reservation, checkout, and background-release workflows, alongside their rejection branches, look like this:

metadata.alt: Reserve with a stock check, checkout with an expiry check and discount, and a background reaper releasing untouched expired reservations

items: Reserve path: reserve item → enough available stock → decrement stock, create a time-bounded reservation.
Reserve rejection path: reserve item → not enough available stock → rejected.
Checkout path: checkout → every reservation still active and unexpired → confirm into an order, apply discount.
Checkout rejection path: checkout → a reservation has expired → release its stock immediately, reject the checkout.
Background path: periodic sweep → any active reservation past expiry that nobody touched → release its stock.

blocks.text: The service exposes a small, intention-revealing API:

items: reserveItem(productId, quantity, currentTime): creates a time-bounded reservation, or throws if stock is insufficient.
checkout(userId, reservationIds, couponCode, currentTime): confirms a set of reservations into an order with a discount applied, or throws if any has expired.
expireReservations(currentTime): a background sweep releasing any active reservation whose expiry has passed.

blocks.text: Three custom exceptions cover the realistic failure modes:

items: OutOfStockException: available stock is less than the requested reservation quantity.
ReservationExpiredException: checkout is attempted after a reservation's expiry has already passed.
InvalidReservationException: an unknown reservation id passed to checkout.

blocks.text: The critical race is two buyers reserving the last available unit of a product at nearly the same moment.

metadata.alt: Two threads racing to reserve the last unit; synchronization ensures only one reservation succeeds and the other is rejected

blocks.text: Synchronizing the stock-check-and-decrement step per product ensures the check and the update happen atomically, so available stock can never go negative even under concurrent reservation attempts.
The pattern choices make several future features low-friction to add:

items: A new discounting scheme (tiered by cart total, buy-one-get-one) is a new DiscountStrategy implementation.
A new notification channel (cart abandonment email, low-stock alert) is a new ShoppingObserver implementation.
Explicit buyer-initiated cancellation can reuse the exact same stock-release logic already built for expiry.
A configurable reservation window per product, rather than one fixed global window, is a small change to how expiresAt is computed at reservation time.
Single Responsibility: Product tracks stock, DiscountStrategy decides pricing, ShoppingObserver reacts to events, each for one reason to change.
Open/Closed: new discounting or notification behavior extends via new classes, not edits to ShoppingService.
Liskov Substitution: any DiscountStrategy or ShoppingObserver implementation can replace another without breaking the service.
Interface Segregation: ShoppingObserver exposes only the four lifecycle callbacks a listener actually needs.
Dependency Inversion: ShoppingService depends on the DiscountStrategy and ShoppingObserver interfaces, not concrete classes.
A checkout attempt exactly at the expiry timestamp is treated as expired, using a strict less-than comparison for validity.
A checkout spanning multiple reservations where only one has expired releases just that one and rejects the whole checkout, rather than partially confirming the others.
A reservation confirmed into an order is never touched by the background reaper again, since it is no longer active.
Two reservations for the same product from different buyers are tracked entirely independently, each with its own expiry.
reserveItem: O(1) for the stock check, decrement, and reservation creation.
checkout: O(k) for k reservations being confirmed in one call.
expireReservations: O(active reservations) per sweep.
Space: O(products + reservations + orders) held in memory.

blocks.text: A relational schema mirrors the in-memory model directly, with foreign keys enforcing referential integrity:

metadata.alt: ER diagram: Product, Reservation, Order, and an OrderItem join

items: An index on Reservation(status, expiresAt) speeds up the background sweep's search for expired-but-still-active reservations.
OrderItem links confirmed reservations to the order they became part of.
Support explicit buyer-initiated cancellation before natural expiry, reusing the existing stock-release logic.
Add coupon usage limits and eligibility rules rather than a flat, unconditional lookup.
Make the reservation window configurable per product or per promotional event.
In a distributed deployment, move stock-decrement locking to a database-level row lock or a distributed lock rather than in-process synchronization.

ShoppingService, including reservation creation, checkout confirmation, and the background expiry sweep:

codes.python:
# Custom exceptions for the realistic failure modes.
class OutOfStockException(Exception): pass
class ReservationExpiredException(Exception): pass
class InvalidReservationException(Exception): pass

# The core orchestrator tying every piece together.
class ShoppingService:
    RESERVATION_WINDOW = 10  # how long a hold lasts, in virtual time units

    def __init__(self, discount_strategy):
        self.products = {}          # productId -> Product
        self.reservations = {}      # reservationId -> Reservation
        self.discount_strategy = discount_strategy  # pluggable discount policy
        self.observers = []           # listeners

    def add_product(self, product):
        self.products[product.product_id] = product  # register a product

    def add_observer(self, observer):
        self.observers.append(observer)  # register a listener

    def reserve_item(self, product_id, quantity, current_time, factory):
        product = self.products[product_id]  # look up product
        if product.available_stock < quantity:  # not enough stock
            for obs in self.observers:
                obs.on_reservation_rejected(product_id, "Out of stock")  # notify
            raise OutOfStockException(f"Not enough stock for {product_id}")
        product.decrease_stock(quantity)  # hold the stock immediately
        reservation_id = factory.next_reservation_id()  # build id
        reservation = Reservation(reservation_id, product_id, quantity, current_time + self.RESERVATION_WINDOW)  # build reservation
        self.reservations[reservation_id] = reservation  # store it
        for obs in self.observers:
            obs.on_reservation_created(reservation)  # notify
        return reservation  # hand back to caller

    def checkout(self, user_id, reservation_ids, coupon_code, current_time, factory):
        subtotal = 0.0  # running subtotal across all confirmed reservations
        for reservation_id in reservation_ids:  # validate every reservation first
            reservation = self.reservations.get(reservation_id)  # look up reservation
            if reservation is None:
                raise InvalidReservationException(f"Unknown reservation: {reservation_id}")
            if current_time >= reservation.expires_at:  # this reservation has expired
                product = self.products[reservation.product_id]  # its product
                product.increase_stock(reservation.quantity)  # release the held stock
                reservation.status = ReservationStatus.EXPIRED  # mark expired
                for obs in self.observers:
                    obs.on_reservation_expired(reservation)  # notify
                raise ReservationExpiredException(f"Reservation {reservation_id} has expired")
            product = self.products[reservation.product_id]  # look up its product for pricing
            subtotal += product.price * reservation.quantity  # add this line's cost
        discount = self.discount_strategy.discount_percent(coupon_code)  # discount fraction from the coupon
        total = subtotal * (1.0-discount)  # final total after discount
        for reservation_id in reservation_ids:  # now confirm every reservation
            self.reservations[reservation_id].status = ReservationStatus.CONFIRMED  # mark confirmed
        order_id = factory.next_order_id()  # build order id
        order = Order(order_id, user_id, total)  # build order
        for obs in self.observers:
            obs.on_order_confirmed(order)  # notify
        return order  # hand back to caller

    def expire_reservations(self, current_time):
        for reservation in self.reservations.values():  # scan every reservation
            if reservation.status == ReservationStatus.ACTIVE and current_time >= reservation.expires_at:
                product = self.products[reservation.product_id]  # its product
                product.increase_stock(reservation.quantity)  # release the held stock
                reservation.status = ReservationStatus.EXPIRED  # mark expired
                for obs in self.observers:
                    obs.on_reservation_expired(reservation)  # notify

items: Why release stock immediately when a lazy check at checkout finds an expired reservation, rather than waiting for the next background sweep? Because the buyer is actively interacting with the system right then, and releasing eagerly means the very next buyer who checks stock sees an accurate, up-to-date number instead of a briefly stale one.

Why check expiry with a strict less-than comparison rather than less-than-or-equal? So the exact expiry timestamp itself is treated as the first invalid moment, an explicit, defensible convention rather than an off-by-one accident.

How would you extend this to support explicit cancellation? Add a cancelReservation method that reuses the exact same stock-release code path as expiry, just triggered by the buyer instead of a timeout.

Temporary time-bounded holds vs permanent locks: a temporary hold protects against overselling during an active checkout without permanently tying up inventory for an abandoned cart, at the cost of needing both a lazy and an eager expiry mechanism to guarantee it is always eventually released.

Lazy plus eager expiry vs eager-only: checking expiry lazily at checkout time gives an immediately accurate answer to the one buyer actively interacting with the system, while the eager background sweep guarantees release even for reservations nobody ever touches again; eager-only would leave abandoned holds stale until the next sweep runs.

Flat percentage coupon lookup vs a rules engine: a flat lookup is simple to implement and test, at the cost of not supporting more sophisticated promotions (tiered discounts, minimum cart value, expiration dates on coupons themselves) that a real storefront would eventually need.
Persist products, reservations, and orders in a relational database rather than in-memory maps, using the schema in the Database Design section.

Emit reservation/order/expiry events to a message queue so downstream systems (inventory alerts, cart abandonment emails, analytics) can consume them asynchronously instead of via in-process observers.
Add idempotency keys to checkout so retried network requests cannot create duplicate orders.
Expose metrics on reservation expiry rate per product, which reveals how often buyers abandon checkout and could inform UX changes to the checkout flow itself.
